k: OES open econometric systems engine what is
a: Open Econometric Systems is a free tool on this site that runs 51 econometric models in your browser: you upload a CSV, choose the model and read the results, and nothing leaves your computer. Every model has a tutorial guide with real output and the Python code behind it.

q: Which model should I use for time series that are not stationary?
k: non-stationary unit root I(1) cointegration choose model decision tree
a: It depends on the unit-root tests. All variables stationary: OLS or local projections. All I(1) and not cointegrated: a VAR in first differences. All I(1) and cointegrated: a VECM. A mix of I(0) and I(1): ARDL, or NARDL if increases and decreases may differ. The Time-Series Guide has a decision tree and a questionnaire that picks the model from your answers.

q: When should I use a threshold regression and when a smooth-transition regression?
k: TAR SETAR LSTAR ESTAR threshold smooth transition nonlinear regime
a: Use a threshold regression (TAR or SETAR) when behaviour changes abruptly once a variable crosses a level, and you want to estimate the level with a bootstrap test and confidence interval. Use a smooth-transition regression (LSTAR or ESTAR) when the change is gradual as a state variable moves through a range. With a very fast transition the two give nearly the same fit, which the smooth-transition guide shows on a Taylor rule.

q: How is a threshold different from a structural break?
k: threshold structural break Bai-Perron regime date level
a: A structural break is tied to a date: the parameters change at some point in time and stay changed. A threshold is tied to the level of a variable: the same regime can occur at several dates whenever the variable is above or below the threshold. The Bai-Perron guide covers breaks and the threshold guide covers thresholds. If the high regime sits in one period, as high inflation does in the 1970s, the two readings can look alike.

q: How do I estimate the effect of a monetary policy shock?
k: impulse response monetary shock SVAR local projections proxy
a: Use a structural VAR or local projections. The SVAR guide identifies shocks by a Cholesky ordering, long-run restrictions (Blanchard-Quah) or an external instrument (proxy-SVAR). The local-projections guide gives impulse responses horizon by horizon without a full system. For Bayesian versions see the Bayesian guide.

k: panel data fixed effects random effects GMM PMG CS-ARDL panel threshold
a: The Panel Data Guide covers pooled OLS, random and fixed effects, GMM, Driscoll-Kraay errors, mean-group and CCE estimators, first differences, pooled mean group, CS-ARDL, panel local projections and Hansen's panel threshold regression, with a decision tree to choose among them.

q: How do I estimate causal effects?
k: causal inference difference in differences regression discontinuity instrumental variables synthetic control
a: The Causal Inference Guide covers difference-in-differences and event studies, regression discontinuity, instrumental variables and related designs, each with code and real output.

q: Is there a guide for Bayesian estimation or Markov-switching models?
a: Yes. The Bayesian Guide covers Bayesian VARs, factor-augmented and time-varying parameter VARs, stochastic volatility and more. The Markov-Switching Guide covers Markov-switching autoregressions, regressions and VARs.

q: Can I run the models on my own data?
k: upload csv own data run browser privacy
a: Yes. Open Econometric Systems runs in your browser: choose a model, upload a CSV, map the columns and run it. The data stay on your computer. Each result can be reproduced with the Python code shown in the model's guide.
